doc.title: John Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Scale wages, first real money with Shearing, and the gift of a bass
summary: Pay was small; Levy's real money came with Shearing; after he stopped playing, Nancy and Joe gave him a bass for his 75th birthday.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: What was scale like back then?
I mean Milt and Joe were talking about that.
Yeah, they probably remember better than I do what it was. But it wasn’t much I’ll tell you that. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
I remember Milt I think was saying that before he joined Cab he was working for $35 a week, and you know then he went with Cab and it tripled and he said, “I’m a millionaire.”

Well I know I worked, I worked in night clubs in Chicago coming along and made $50 a week, and that was, that was big money, you know? It wasn’t big money, it was just enough to get by on, but my first experience of really making money was really with George Shearing because up to that point, even with Buddy Rich and with the Stuff Smith things was pretty good, but the real money, the real money came with — for me — came with George Shearing, and then of course the experience and all that. But I was fortunate, yeah, as I say, very, very, very lucky in my relationships with the playing days. Because from, I was always with the very best people, you know. It was always, whatever the dollar was it was top dollar. And I was very independent and I didn’t travel much. My move from Chicago to New York was the biggest move and I never went back. I moved my family and everything to New York. And after I’d been there for a while and I realized I wasn’t going to go back to Chicago to live. And I worked all the time, from one group to the next and the next, and just until I got into this end of the business. And a lot of people ask me, “don’t you miss playing?” I say I did at the beginning. I used to go around and sort of really miss it, and sit in whenever I could. And I did that for maybe two or three years after. Then I got so busy I didn’t have time to do that, and didn’t even own a bass. And for my 75th birthday, Nancy and Joe got together and had got a bass for me. They gave me that as a birthday present.
Maybe they were trying to tell me something.
Just in case you don’t have a job as a manager any time soon, maybe you’ll need this, huh?
Maybe they was trying to tell me, “you better go back to this.”
